newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: BHP hobbled by weak prices.
newsitem.headline: BHP hobbled by weak prices.

text.p: Australian resources giant The Broken Hill Proprietary Co on Friday announced a 23 percent drop in first quarter net profit, blaming a strong Australian dollar for exacerbating the impact of weak copper and steel markets.
The steel, petroleum and copper giant reported a net profit of A$287 million for the three months to August 31, down from A$372 million a year earlier.
The result was within market expectations.
Managing director John Prescott put a brave face on lower result, claiming the company was set to improve.
"What we have to do is to strengthen those foundations in the short term by improving our near-term performance," he said.

"That's going to require a great deal of effort, a great deal of intensity. It must be done," he said in a pre-recorded interview prepared by the company. Prescott later declined to discuss the financial outlook for the current quarter.
Analysts have been trimming back their BHP earnings estimates due to weaker copper prices and a flat steel market.

However, although the result was within market expectations, it was not enough to stop BHP's share price falling. By the close of Friday's dealings, BHP shares were five cents down at A$16.04. The stock has fallen about 15 percent since May.

"I tend to feel that overall the result hasn't changed our outlook for the company ... that things will be a little bit subdued while the steel markets and copper markets are subdued," one Sydney-based analyst told Reuters.
BHP results were largely hit by copper, a metal in which BHP invested heavily earlier this year before copper prices plummeted on the Sumitomo copper trading scandal in May.
Prescott said the full impact of the alleged rogue trading already had passed through the market but he noted confidence was yet to return.
"We believe the fundamentals for the copper market are somewhat better than the market pricing indicates," he added.
BHP's copper division reported a 56 percent fall in net profit to A$85 million for the first quarter, despite increased copper sales.
BHP became the world's second largest copper producer when it bought the U.S.-based Magma Copper Co for US$2.4 billion in January.

While Prescott was forced to admit the Magma business had posted a loss for the quarter, he did not quantify it and said the group had set aggressive targets for cost savings in its copper and other divisions.
Quarterly profits fell 38 percent to A$90 million at BHP Steel, the troubled division which hobbled the group's financial performance for fiscal 1995/96.
The company noted that despite a flat Australian market for steel during the period, signs of improving domestic steel demand were emerging.

BHP's total sales rose a marginal 2.7 percent to A$4.84 billion in the quarter. Sales growth was constrained by a stronger Australian dollar, which rose to an average 79 U.S. cents from 73 U.S. cents a year earlier.
BHP noted that a one cent increase in the Australian dollar cuts about A$35 million from its bottom line.
Of the four key divisions -- steel, petroleum, copper and minerals -- only the petroleum group increased profit.
-- Melbourne bureau 61-3 9286-1435
